strengths: Introduces CodeFlowBench, a large-scale benchmark (5,258 Codeforces problems) specifically targeting multi-turn, iterative code generation with function-level dependency structures and unit tests. The setting is under-evaluated and practically relevant.

Provides a detailed, automated data-curation pipeline built on official Codeforces editorials and verified submissions, with promising support for continuous benchmark updates and reduced reliance on noisy user solutions.

Proposes an evaluation framework that goes beyond aggregate pass@1, including multi-turn and single-turn patterns, structural labels (Overall-Turns, Overall-Depth, DSC), and the Average Pass Depth metric to analyze where in the dependency tree models fail.
Reports extensive experiments across 15 closed- and open-source models, consistently showing a substantial multi-turn vs. single-turn performance gap and depth/structural-complexity effects.

The error taxonomy (Incomplete Reasoning, Insufficient Globalization, Instruction Misinterpretation) and accompanying case studies provide useful qualitative insights into model failures in sequential code reuse.
The paper is clearly written, well structured, and the appendices contain useful pipeline details, prompts, and examples that aid understanding of the benchmark construction.
The work has clear relevance to computational linguistics and NLP, especially for code generation, benchmarking, and evaluation of LLM agents in multi-step programming workflows.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction relies heavily on LLMs (DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3) for solution generation, subproblem decomposition, natural-language subproblem descriptions, and code conversion. There is no human validation or inter-annotator agreement reported, so subproblem quality, statement clarity, and decomposition consistency are not established.

Subproblem unit tests are generated by instrumenting a single editorial solution and capturing input-output pairs at function invocations. This can yield biased or incomplete coverage, may not cover edge cases or alternative correct implementations, and does not guarantee that a function is fully correct under a broader contract. The test suite quality is not independently validated.

Potential data contamination is a serious unresolved concern: Codeforces problems and editorials are public and likely included in LLM pretraining data. Selecting the most recent 20% of problems is not a rigorous contamination-free split; no model training cutoffs, overlap analysis, or decontamination study is reported, which threatens the validity of the reported pass rates.

Reproducibility is currently limited. The code and dataset are promised to be available, but no artifact is provided in the submission. The pipeline depends on web scraping, Codeforces APIs, and proprietary/large LLM APIs, and exact evaluation settings, decoding parameters, and submission-bot robustness are not fully specified.

The 'multi-turn/iterative' setting is closer to sequential one-pass function generation than iterative refinement: models receive no execution feedback after a failed subproblem, are stopped on failure, and must follow one canonical decomposition derived from a single editorial solution. This may over-constrain evaluation and does not fully capture real-world iterative debugging or alternative valid modularizations.

The multi-turn vs. single-turn comparison is potentially confounded by the additional constraints of the multi-turn setting (sequential dependency, reuse of specified functions, no global plan). The paper also reports only Pass@1 without repeated sampling, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so small model differences and rankings are uncertain.
Some claims, such as 'first benchmark' and 'eliminate potential data leakage,' are stronger than the presented evidence and need more careful qualification.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant gap: multi-turn, iterative, modular code generation with function reuse is underexplored relative to single-turn code generation benchmarks.

It curates a sizeable set of 5,258 competitive-programming problems and uses official Codeforces editorials plus judge verification for solution-code filtering, which is a reasonable quality-control step at the solution level.

The proposed evaluation includes multi-turn and single-turn patterns, plus dependency-aware metrics (APD, DSC) and an error taxonomy (IR, IG, IM) that could provide useful analysis directions if validated.
The experiments cover a broad range of closed- and open-source models and reveal a consistent multi-turn performance gap, which is a plausible and interesting empirical signal.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is seriously inadequate: the paper states code and dataset will be available soon, but no dataset, code, evaluation harness, or pipeline artifacts are released with the submission. The benchmark cannot be verified, and many claims depend on proprietary LLM APIs and an automated Codeforces submission bot.

The central APD metric is internally inconsistent or at least unclearly defined. With depth counted from the root (root=0), the formula PD = D - d - 1 yields negative values for errors on leaf subproblems, and the reported APD values cannot be reconciled with the formula. Since APD is a primary evaluation metric, this undermines the experimental conclusions.

Subproblem unit tests are derived by instrumenting executions on Codeforces public/sample tests, not from hidden or exhaustive test suites. Coverage per subproblem is not validated, and many subproblems may receive few or no meaningful test cases, making turn-level and APD results unreliable.

The benchmark construction relies heavily on LLM-generated artifacts: DeepSeek-R1 converts editorial text/solutions into executable code, and DeepSeek-V3 generates subproblem descriptions. DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-R1 are then evaluated on the same benchmark, creating contamination/self-preference risks. No quality validation or inter-annotator agreement is reported for these generated components.

The multi-turn setting is artificial relative to real codeflow: the dependency tree, turn order, subproblem decomposition, and function signatures are provided from a known solution. Models do not discover decomposition or reuse opportunities; they implement prescribed functions sequentially. This limits claims about comprehensively evaluating real iterative codeflow.

The paper does not empirically compare against related multi-turn or dependency-aware benchmarks (e.g., InterCode, MTPB, CodeEvalPro, TreeInstruct, LiveCodeBench) despite claiming existing benchmarks lack these capabilities. The novelty argument is therefore qualitative rather than demonstrated.

Evaluation is based on only the most recent 20% of problems, with no contamination analysis or statistical uncertainty estimates. No confidence intervals are given for pass@1/APD, and manual error analyses in Tables 2 and 3 lack sample sizes, annotation guidelines, or reliability measures.

The single-turn versus multi-turn comparison does not control for information differences or error propagation. Multi-turn stops after the first error, which mechanically lowers pass rates; this does not by itself isolate multi-turn ability from sequential error sensitivity.

The paper overclaims 'first' and 'comprehensive' benchmark status while omitting key validation of the pipeline, subproblem tests, and metric behavior. The error taxonomy and remediation-rate analysis are based on small, manually annotated samples and do not yet support strong causal conclusions.

strengths: The paper targets an important and relatively underexplored setting: dependency-aware, multi-turn code generation where models must reuse previously implemented functions, which is relevant to real software engineering and code-focused NLP.

It introduces a large benchmark resource with two complementary components: CodeFlowBench-Comp (5,258 competitive-programming problems) and CodeFlowBench-Repo (real-world GitHub-based domains), broadening evaluation beyond isolated function synthesis.

The data-curation pipeline is technically substantial: AST-based function dependency parsing, topological subproblem generation, test-case instrumentation, and Codeforces-based verification of canonical solutions.

The evaluation framework contributes structural diagnostics (Pass Turn, Pass Depth, APD, APT, DSC) beyond final Pass@1, which allows finer-grained analysis of where models fail in the dependency hierarchy.
The experimental study covers 19 closed- and open-source models, demonstrating consistent multi-turn degradation and depth-wise performance trends across two benchmark subsets.
The error analysis into Incomplete Reasoning, Insufficient Globalization, and Instruction Misinterpretation provides actionable insight into failure modes of current code LLMs.
The appendix includes detailed prompts, pipeline descriptions, cost estimates, and dataset statistics, showing strong potential as a reproducible benchmark resource if released.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is not sufficiently clear for competitive-programming tasks: it is not stated whether model outputs are judged with Codeforces hidden tests or only with public tests. If only public tests are used, Pass@1 may substantially overestimate algorithmic correctness and weaken the central claims.

Subproblem unit tests are generated by instrumenting the canonical solution on public tests, which may miss edge cases, leave some functions untested, or overfit to one valid implementation; test coverage and sufficiency are not empirically validated.

The 'multi-turn, iterative' framing is overstated. Turns follow a fixed topological order from the canonical solution, and the workflow stops on failure rather than allowing feedback, revision, or interactive debugging; this is closer to sequential one-shot function generation than true iterative codeflow.

Data contamination is not adequately controlled. Codeforces problems, official editorials, and GitHub code are likely in LLM pretraining data; the 'most recent 1,000' Comp subset does not guarantee decontamination, and the Repo subset is not checked for leakage.

Several proposed metrics (PT, PD, APT, APD, DSC) are complex and not clearly defined in the main paper; Table 2 is difficult to interpret, and no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests accompany the main model comparisons.
The paper derives @k estimators for APD and APT, but main experiments report only APD@1/APT@1, so the proposed @k framework is not actually exercised in the primary results.

Table 5 reports identical structural complexity metrics across solutions generated by different LLMs (2.08 turns, 1.94 depth for all), which is surprising and either indicates an unclear experimental design or raises concerns about how solution generation was controlled.

The dataset construction relies heavily on LLM-based conversion, back-translation, and description generation; while an ablation is provided, there is no full human validation of subproblem descriptions, generated tests, or decomposition correctness at scale.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of a code/data release link. Although the appendix provides prompts and pipeline descriptions, the actual benchmark, test harness, and evaluation artifacts are not available for independent verification.

The multi-turn versus single-turn comparison may be confounded: single-turn models receive all subproblem descriptions at once, while multi-turn models receive only the current turn and prior code, so the measured gap reflects global planning and information access as well as multi-turn capability.
The manual error analysis lacks details on sample size, sampling strategy, and inter-annotator agreement, making the error distribution in Table 3 difficult to assess reliably.

The paper claims periodic updates to mitigate contamination, but the experiments evaluate only a static snapshot and provide no evidence that the update mechanism was used or that it improves benchmark validity.

No comparison to strong iterative/agentic baselines (e.g., self-repair, execution-feedback loops, or multi-agent workflows) is provided, limiting the practical interpretation of the reported multi-turn performance gap.
